en: Thus have I heard: the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta (The Greater Discourse on the Destruction of Craving), the thirty-eighth in the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a pernicious view had arisen in a monk named Sāti, the son of a fisherman, as follows:
“As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, not another.”
A number of bhikkhus heard:
“It seems that such an evil speculative view has arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, not another.’”
Then those bhikkhus approached the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman; having approached, they said this to the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:
“Is it true, friend Sāti, that such an evil speculative view has arisen in you:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, and there is no other’?”
“Indeed, friends, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that this very same consciousness runs on and transmigrates, and not another.
Then those bhikkhus, wishing to detach the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman, from that evil speculative view, pressed him, questioned him, and cross-examined him:
“Do not say so, friend Sāti; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak in such a way.”
"In many ways, friend Sāti, consciousness has been described by the Blessed One as dependently arisen; apart from conditions, there is no origination of consciousness.
Even though the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, was thus being pressed, cross-examined, and rebuked by those bhikkhus, he stubbornly adhered to and insisted upon that same evil view, declaring:
“Indeed, friends, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the cycle of rebirths, and not another.

When those bhikkhus were unable to detach the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman, from this pernicious view, they then approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they [reported this to] the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, a pernicious view such as this has arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman:
'As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, and it is not another.'"
“Venerable sir, we indeed heard that such an evil speculative view had arisen in the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, and it is not another.
Then, venerable sir, we approached the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman, and having approached, we said this to the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman:”
“Is it true, friend Sāti, that such an evil view as this has arisen in you:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, not another’?
When this was said, venerable sir, the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, said this to us:
"Friends, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that this very same consciousness runs on and transmigrates, and not another.
Then, venerable sir, wishing to detach the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman, from this pernicious view, we questioned him, cross-examined him, and pressed him for an explanation:
"Do not say so, friend Sāti; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak in such a way."
"In many ways, friend Sāti, consciousness has been described by the Blessed One as dependently arisen; apart from conditions, there is no arising of consciousness.

Even so, Bhante, when the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, was being cross-examined, interrogated, and rebuked by us, he stubbornly and obstinately clung to that same evil view and continued to assert it: [as before].
“Indeed, friends, it is thus that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: this very same consciousness runs on and wanders about, not another.
“Venerable sir, since we were unable to detach the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman, from this pernicious view, we have come to inform the Blessed One of this matter.
Then the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikkhu:
“Come, bhikkhu, address the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, in my name, saying:
‘Friend Sāti, the Teacher calls you.
“Yes, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu replied to the Blessed One. He then approached the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, and having approached him, spoke thus to the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman:
“The Teacher calls you, friend Sāti.
“Very well, friend,” the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, replied to that bhikkhu.
He then approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. To one side...
As the bhikkhu Sāti, son of a fisherman, was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Is it true, Sāti, that such an evil speculative view has arisen in you:
‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is this very same consciousness that runs and wanders through the round of rebirths, and it is nothing other than this’?”
“Venerable sir, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: that very same consciousness runs on and transmigrates, and not another.
“But what, Sāti, is that consciousness?
“That which, venerable sir, speaks and experiences, and which here and there experiences the result of good and evil deeds.”
“Whose teaching is it, you foolish man, that you understand me to have taught in this way?
Have I not, you foolish man, in many ways stated that consciousness is dependently arisen, and that apart from conditions there is no coming-into-being of consciousness?
Yet you, foolish man, by your own misapprehension both misrepresent us and injure yourself, and generate much demerit.”
"For that, foolish man, will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"What do you think, bhikkhus?"
“Could it be, Sāti, that this bhikkhu Kevaṭṭaputta has even kindled a spark of faith in this Dhamma and Vinaya?
“How could it be so, Bhante?
Certainly not, Bhante.”
When this was said, the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman, sat silent, ashamed, with shoulders drooping and head bowed, brooding and speechless.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving that the bhikkhu Sāti, the son of a fisherman, was silent, ashamed, with shoulders drooping and head bowed, brooding and speechless, said to him:
"Foolish man, you will be known by this evil view of your own."
"In this matter, monks, I shall question you.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:

"Monks, do you also understand the Dhamma taught by me in the same way that this monk Sāti, son of a fisherman, through his own misapprehension, misrepresents us, injures himself, and generates much demerit?"
“No, venerable sir.
For in many ways, venerable sir, consciousness has been described by the Blessed One as dependently arisen; apart from conditions, there is no origination of consciousness.
“Excellent, excellent, monks!”
“It is good, monks, that you understand the Dhamma taught by me in this way.
For in many ways, monks, have I told you that consciousness is dependently arisen; apart from conditions, there is no arising of consciousness.
Yet this monk Sāti, son of a fisherman, through his own misapprehension, misrepresents both us and himself, injures himself, and generates much demerit.
For that will lead to the misfortune and suffering of that foolish man for a long time.
"Monks, whatever condition dependent upon which consciousness arises, by that very [condition] it is reckoned as 'consciousness.
Dependent upon the eye and forms, consciousness arises; it is reckoned simply as 'eye-consciousness.'"
Dependent on the ear and sounds, consciousness arises; it is reckoned simply as "ear-consciousness.
Dependent on the nose and odors, consciousness arises; it is reckoned simply as "nose-consciousness.
Dependent on the tongue and flavors, consciousness arises; it is reckoned simply as "tongue-consciousness."
Dependent on the body and tangible objects, consciousness arises; it is designated simply as "body-consciousness.
Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, consciousness arises; it is designated simply as "mind-consciousness.
Just as, monks, whatever condition a fire burns in dependence upon, by that very thing it is designated.
Fire burns dependent on wood and is reckoned simply as "wood-fire";
fire burns dependent on splinters and is reckoned simply as "splinter-fire";
fire burns dependent on grass and is reckoned simply as "grass-fire."
Fire burns dependent on cow dung and is reckoned simply as a cow-dung fire;
fire burns dependent on chaff and is reckoned simply as a chaff fire;
fire burns dependent on rubbish and is reckoned simply as a rubbish fire.
In the same way, monks, whatever condition consciousness arises dependent upon, by that very name it is designated.
Consciousness arises dependent on the eye and forms; it is designated simply as "eye-consciousness.
Consciousness arises dependent on the ear and sounds; it is designated simply as "ear-consciousness."
Dependent on the nose and odors, consciousness arises; it is designated simply as "nose-consciousness.
Dependent on the tongue and tastes, consciousness arises; it is designated simply as "tongue-consciousness.
Dependent on the body and tactile objects, consciousness arises; it is designated simply as "body-consciousness."
“Dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, consciousness arises; it is reckoned simply as ‘mind-consciousness.
Do you see, bhikkhus, that this has come to be?”—“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Do you see, monks, that it arises conditioned by that nutriment?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”—
“Do you see, monks, that what has come to be through the cessation of that nutriment is subject to cessation?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Does doubt arise, bhikkhus, for one who is uncertain whether this has come to be or not?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, does doubt arise in one who is uncertain: ‘Could it be that what has come into being through the arising of that nutriment does not exist?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Bhikkhus, does doubt arise in one who is uncertain: ‘Could it be that with the cessation of that nutriment, what has come into being is subject to cessation? “Yes, venerable sir.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Bhikkhus, when one sees with correct wisdom as it really is: ‘This has come to be,’ is doubt abandoned?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, when one sees with correct wisdom, as it really is, that ‘this has its origin from nutriment,’ is doubt abandoned?”—

“Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus, when one sees with correct wisdom, as it really is, that ‘with the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is subject to cessation,’ is doubt abandoned?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“‘This has come to be,’ bhikkhus—do you have no doubt about this?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, are you free from doubt regarding this: ‘It is from that nutriment that these beings come into being’?”—“Yes, venerable sir.”—“Bhikkhus, are you free from doubt regarding this:
‘With the cessation of that nutriment, whatever has come to be is subject to cessation’?”—“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“‘This has come to be,’ bhikkhus—has this been well seen with right wisdom as it actually is?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, has it been well seen with right wisdom, as it really is, that ‘this arises conditioned by that nutriment’?”—
“Yes, venerable sir. “Bhikkhus,
has it been well seen with right wisdom, as it really is, that ‘with the cessation of that nutriment, whatever has come to be is subject to cessation’?”— “Yes, venerable sir.”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Bhikkhus, if you were to cling to this view— which is thus purified and thus cleansed— cherish it, treasure it,
and treat it as ‘mine,’ would you then understand the Dhamma taught by me as being like a raft?”
“Is it for the sake of crossing over, not for the sake of grasping?”—
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”—
“If you, monks, do not cling to this view, which is thus purified and thus cleansed...”
“Monks, you should not cherish it, you should not long for it, you should not treat it as ‘mine.
Do you understand, monks, that I have taught the Dhamma as being like a raft, for the purpose of crossing over and not for the purpose of grasping?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have come to be, or for the assistance of those seeking rebirth.
What are the four?
Edible food, whether gross or subtle; second, contact; third, mental volition; fourth, consciousness.”
"And what, monks, are these four nutriments caused by, what is their origin, from what are they born, and from what do they arise?
These four nutriments have craving as their cause, craving as their origin, craving as their birth, and craving as their source.
And this craving, monks, is caused by what, has what as its origin, is born from what, and arises from what?"
Craving has feeling as its source, feeling as its origin, feeling as its birth, and feeling as its provenance.
And what, monks, is the source of this feeling, what is its origin, what is its birth, what is its provenance?
Feeling has contact as its source, contact as its origin, contact as its birth, and contact as its provenance.
"And what, monks, is this contact: what is its source, what is its origin, from what is it born, from what does it arise?
Contact has the six sense bases as its source, the six sense bases as its origin; it is born from the six sense bases and arises from the six sense bases.
And what, monks, is this sixfold base: what is its source, what is its origin, from what is it born, from what does it arise?"
The six sense bases have name-and-form as their source, name-and-form as their origin, name-and-form as their birth, and name-and-form as their arising.
And what, monks, is the source of this name-and-form, what its origin, what its birth, and what its arising?
Name-and-form has consciousness as its source, consciousness as its origin, consciousness as its birth, and consciousness as its arising.
“Bhikkhus, what is the source of this consciousness? What is its origin? From what is it born? From what does it arise?
Consciousness has volitional formations as its source, volitional formations as its origin; it is born from volitional formations and arises from volitional formations.
And what, bhikkhus, is the source of these volitional formations? What is their origin? From what are they born? From what do they arise?”
Volitional formations have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their origin, ignorance as their birth, and ignorance as their arising.
Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations;
with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness.
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact.
With contact as condition, feeling arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises.
With clinging as condition, existence comes to be;
with existence as condition, birth;
and with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
"Thus there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
'With birth as condition, aging-and-death come to be'—this, indeed, has been said.
But, bhikkhus, is it with birth as condition that aging-and-death come to be, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?"
“Venerable sir, aging-and-death has birth as its condition;
this is how it occurs to us here:
‘Aging-and-death has birth as its condition.’”
“It has been said: ‘With existence as condition, birth.
Now, monks, does birth have existence as its condition, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Birth, venerable sir, has existence as its condition.”
Thus it occurs to us here:
"With existence as condition, there is birth.
Furthermore, it has been said: "With clinging as condition, there is existence."
“Monks, is existence conditioned by clinging, or is it not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, existence is conditioned by clinging;
this is how it stands in this matter.”
“With clinging as condition, existence comes to be.
“It has been said, ‘With craving as condition, clinging. Now, monks, does clinging have craving as its condition, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Clinging, venerable sir, has craving as its condition.”
Thus it occurs to us here:
"With craving as condition, there is clinging.
Furthermore, it has been said: "With feeling as condition, there is craving."
“Bhikkhus, is craving conditioned by feeling or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Craving is conditioned by feeling, venerable sir;
this is how it stands in this matter.”
“With feeling as condition, craving arises.
“It has been said, ‘With contact as condition, feeling arises.
Now, monks, does feeling arise with contact as its condition, or not? Or how is it in this case?”
“Venerable sir, feeling has contact as its condition;
this is how it appears to us here:
‘Feeling has contact as its condition.’”
“It has been said: ‘With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.
Now, monks, does contact indeed have the six sense bases as its condition, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, contact does have the six sense bases as its condition.”
Thus it occurs to us here:
"With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises.
Furthermore, it has been said: "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise."
“Bhikkhus, is it conditioned by name-and-form that the six sense bases come to be, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, it is conditioned by name-and-form that the six sense bases come to be;
this is how it stands in this matter.”
“With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases [arise].
“It has been said, ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form.
Now, monks, does name-and-form have consciousness as its condition, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?”
“With consciousness as condition, venerable sir, there is name-and-form;
thus it occurs to us here:
‘With consciousness as condition, there is name-and-form.’”
“It has been said: ‘With volitional formations as condition, consciousness.
Now, monks, does consciousness have volitional formations as its condition, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Consciousness has volitional formations as its condition, venerable sir.”
"Thus it occurs to us here:
'With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises.
"It has indeed been said: 'With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise.'"
“Bhikkhus, are volitional formations conditioned by ignorance or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Volitional formations are conditioned by ignorance, venerable sir;
this is how it stands for us in this matter.”
“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise. “Excellent, monks!
Thus, monks, you too say this, and I also say this:”
When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. That is to say:
with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises.
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact.
With contact as condition, feeling arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises.
With clinging as condition, existence comes to be;
with existence as condition, birth;
and with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness.
With the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form;
with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact.
With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging.
With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence;
with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth;
with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
"Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
'With the cessation of birth comes the cessation of aging and death'—this has been said.
But, monks, does the cessation of aging and death come about through the cessation of birth, or not? Or how is it in this regard?"
“With the cessation of birth, venerable sir, there is the cessation of aging and death;
this is how it occurs to us here:
with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.”
“It has been said: ‘With the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth.
Now, monks, does the cessation of birth come about through the cessation of existence, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, the cessation of birth comes about through the cessation of existence.”
Thus it occurs to us here:
"With the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth.
Furthermore, it has been said: "With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence."
“Bhikkhus, does the cessation of existence follow from the cessation of clinging, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, the cessation of existence follows from the cessation of clinging;
such is our understanding in this matter.”
“With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence.
“It has been said: ‘With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging.
Now, monks, does the cessation of clinging come about through the cessation of craving, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?”
“With the cessation of craving, venerable sir, there is the cessation of clinging;
thus it occurs to us here:
‘With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging.’”
“It has been said: ‘With the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving.
Now, monks, does the cessation of craving come about with the cessation of feeling, or not? How is this so?
“With the cessation of feeling, venerable sir, comes the cessation of craving.”
Thus it occurs to us here:
"With the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving.
"It has indeed been said: 'With the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling.'"
“Monks, does the cessation of feeling come about through the cessation of contact, or not? Or how do you understand this?
“Venerable sir, the cessation of feeling comes about through the cessation of contact;
this is how we understand it.”
“With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
“It has been said: ‘With the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact.
Now, monks, does the cessation of the six sense bases lead to the cessation of contact, or not? What is the case here?”
“With the cessation of the six sense bases, venerable sir, there is the cessation of contact;
this is how it occurs to us here:
with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact.”
“It has been said: ‘With the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases.
Now, monks, does the cessation of the six sense bases come about through the cessation of name-and-form, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, the cessation of the six sense bases comes about through the cessation of name-and-form.”
Thus it occurs to us here:
"With the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases.
"It has indeed been said: 'With the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form.'"
“Bhikkhus, does the cessation of name-and-form follow from the cessation of consciousness, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, the cessation of name-and-form follows from the cessation of consciousness;
this is how it stands in this matter.”
“With the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form.
“It has been said: ‘With the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness.
Now, monks, does the cessation of consciousness occur with the cessation of volitional formations, or not? Or how is it in this case?”
“With the cessation of volitional formations, venerable sir, there is the cessation of consciousness;
thus it occurs to us here:
with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness.”
“It has been said: ‘With the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations.
Now, monks, does the cessation of volitional formations come about through the cessation of ignorance, or not? Or how does it stand in this matter?
“Venerable sir, the cessation of volitional formations comes about through the cessation of ignorance.”
“This is how it occurs to us here:
with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
“Good, bhikkhus.”
Thus, monks, you too should say this, and I also say this:
when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say:
with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations.
With the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness;
with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form;
with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases.
With the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases;
with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases.
With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging;
with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence;
with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth.
With the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

Monks, knowing and seeing thus, would you run back toward the past, thinking: [“Were we in the past? Or were we not in the past? What were we in the past? How were we in the past? Having been what, what did we become in the past?”]?”
“Did we exist in the past? Or did we not exist in the past? What were we in the past? How were we in the past? Having been what, what did we become in the past?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Monks, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you run back toward the future limit, thinking:
‘Shall we exist in the future? Shall we not exist in the future? What shall we be in the future?’”
“Will we indeed exist in the future? How will we indeed exist in the future?
Having been what, what will we indeed become in the future?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you now, in the present time, have any doubt within yourselves as to whether:
‘Do I exist? Or do I not exist? What am I? How am I? From where has this being come, and where will it go?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you say:
‘The Teacher is venerable to us; out of reverence for the Teacher we speak thus’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you say:
‘The ascetic says this, and we, being ascetics, say the same’?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you point to another teacher?”—

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”— “Bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you adhere to those vows, ceremonies, and auspicious rites of the various ascetics and brahmins as being essential?”— “Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“No, venerable sir.
“Is it not the case, bhikkhus, that you speak only of what you yourselves have known, seen, and understood?
“Yes, venerable sir.”

“Excellent, bhikkhus! You have been well-guided by me, bhikkhus, through this Dhamma that is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves.
‘This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise for themselves’—it is with reference to this that it was said.”
“Monks, the descent of the embryo occurs through the conjunction of three things.
Here, the mother and father have come together, but the mother is not in her season, and the *gandhabba* is not present; as long as this is so, there is no descent of the embryo.
Here, the mother and father have come together, and the mother is in her season, but the *gandhabba* is not present; as long as this is so, there is no descent of the embryo.”

But when, monks, the mother and father come together, and the mother is in her season, and the gandhabba is present—thus, through the coming together of these three, there is the descent into the womb.
Then, monks, the mother carries that embryo in her womb for nine or ten months as a heavy burden with great risk.
Then, monks, after the lapse of nine or ten months, the mother gives birth to it as a heavy burden with great risk.
As soon as he is born, she nourishes him with her own blood;
for in the discipline of the Noble One, monks, mother’s milk is indeed called "blood.
Then, monks, as that boy grows up and his faculties reach maturity...
He plays with those toys for children, namely: a toy plough, a toy cart, a spinning top, a whirling disk, a toy measure, a toy chariot, and a toy bow.
Then, monks, as that boy grows up and his faculties reach maturity, he enjoys himself, provided and endowed with the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … [and so forth].
...by means of tastes cognizable by the tongue ...
and by means of tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.

Having seen a form with the eye, he becomes infatuated with forms that are pleasing, and he feels aversion toward forms that are unpleasing; he dwells with unestablished mindfulness of the body and with a limited mind.
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.

Thus, having fallen into attraction and aversion, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains attached to it.
As he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, delight arises in him.

Whatever delight there is in feelings, that is clinging; with that clinging as condition, existence comes to be; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.
Having heard a sound with the ear... [and so on].
Having smelled an odor with the nose … pe … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … pe … having touched a tangible object with the body … pe …

Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one becomes attached to agreeable phenomena and feels aversion toward disagreeable phenomena; one dwells with unestablished mindfulness of the body and with a limited mind.
And one does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.

Thus, having fallen into attraction and repulsion, whatever feeling one experiences—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—one delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains clinging to it.
As he delights in that feeling, welcomes it, and remains attached to it, delight arises. That delight in feelings is clinging;
with that clinging as condition, there is becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; and with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be.
Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering.

"Here, monks, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing."
He proclaims the holy life, which is entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Endowed with that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
“Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is the open air.
It is not easy for one living at home to practice the holy life in its complete perfection, in its total purity, polished like a conch shell.”
"What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth,
and having abandoned a small or large circle of kinsmen, he shaves off his hair and beard.
Having clothed himself in saffron robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life and abstains from taking life;
with rod laid aside and weapon laid aside, modest, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings, he dwells.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft and pure.
Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of chastity; he dwells apart, abstaining from sexual intercourse and the vulgar ways of the village.
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he is a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech. Having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people;
nor, having heard something there, does he repeat it here for the purpose of dividing those people.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united. Delighting in concord, rejoicing in concord, finding joy in concord, he speaks words that create concord.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-pleasing, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.

Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the Vinaya; he speaks at the proper time words that are worth treasuring, accompanied by reasons, orderly, and connected with the goal.
He abstains from injuring seeds and plants.
He eats but one meal a day, refrains from eating at night, and abstains from eating at improper times.
He abstains from watching dancing, singing, music, and theatrical performances;
he abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes and unguents, and from adorning or beautifying himself with cosmetics and ornaments.
He abstains from high and luxurious beds;
he abstains from accepting gold and silver;
he abstains from accepting raw grain.
He abstains from accepting raw meat;
he abstains from accepting women and girls;
he abstains from accepting male and female slaves.
He abstains from accepting goats and sheep;
he abstains from accepting chickens and pigs;
he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares.
He abstains from accepting fields and lands;
he abstains from the practice of running errands and acting as a messenger;
he abstains from buying and selling.
He abstains from cheating with scales, cheating with measures, and cheating with weights;
he abstains from bribery, deception, and fraud;
he abstains from mutilation, execution, imprisonment, robbery, plunder, and violence.
Thus he is content with robes that serve to protect the body and almsfood that serves to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these with him.

Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies with its wings as its only burden, even so a bhikkhu is content with robes that serve to protect the body and almsfood that serves to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these with him.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness of blamelessness.
Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
For if he were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when he has heard a sound with the ear... or smelled an odor with the nose... unwholesome states such as covetousness and dejection were to flow in, he practices for its restraint; he guards the eye faculty and attains restraint over the eye faculty.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose... [he practices for its restraint].
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible object with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and dejection might flow into one who dwells with this faculty of mind unrestrained, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of mind and achieves restraint over the faculty of mind.
Endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself the unsullied happiness.
Thus, he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent,
he acts with clear comprehension. Thus, being endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue,
this noble contentment, this noble restraint of the sense faculties, and this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, [he dwells].
He resorts to a secluded lodging: the forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having returned from his almsround after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, and purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind calmed within, and purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Furthermore, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal serenity and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
… [as before] … he enters and dwells in the third jhāna … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.

Thus, having seen a form with the eye, he is not infatuated with a pleasing form and does not feel aversion toward an unpleasing form; he dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind of immeasurable range.
He understands, as it truly is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.

Having thus abandoned both attraction and repulsion, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he does not delight in that feeling, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.
For one who does not delight in that feeling, does not welcome it, and does not remain attached to it, whatever craving there was for feelings ceases.

With the cessation of that craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Thus occurs the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
Having heard a sound with the ear …pe… having smelled an odor with the nose …pe… having tasted a flavor with the tongue …pe…
Having touched a tangible object with the body …pe… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
one is not infatuated with agreeable phenomena and does not feel aversion toward disagreeable phenomena. One dwells with mindfulness established in the body and with a mind immeasurable,
and one understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil unwholesome states cease without remainder.

Thus, having abandoned both attraction and aversion, whatever feeling he feels—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he does not delight in that feeling, does not welcome it, and does not remain clinging to it.
As he does not delight in, welcome, or remain clinging to that feeling, whatever craving there was for feelings ceases in him.

With the cessation of delight comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.

Monks, you should remember this liberation through the destruction of craving in brief as taught by me; but as for the monk Sāti, son of a fisherman, he is still caught in the great net of craving, entangled in the snare of craving.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the eighth, is finished.
